q: Explain self-attention in two sentences.
short: Each token forms a query, compares it by dot product with every token's key (scaled by √d), and softmaxes the scores into weights. Its output is the weighted sum of the value vectors; a causal mask prevents attending to future tokens in decoders.
detail: Multi-head runs this in parallel subspaces.

q: Compute for 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens?
short: 6 × 7×10¹⁰ × 1.4×10¹² ≈ 5.9×10²³ FLOPs (20 tokens per parameter).
detail: 6 = 2 forward + 4 backward per parameter per token.

q: Name the four architecture upgrades in modern LLM blocks.
short: Pre-norm with RMSNorm, rotary position embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU feed-forward layers, and (in some models) Mixture of Experts.
detail: Plus GQA for serving.
follow: Which matters most for long context?

q: Why is memory the recurring bottleneck?
short: Training holds weights, gradients, optimizer states and activations (16 B/param plus activations); attention materialises n² scores; decoding reads all weights and the KV cache every step, so bandwidth and capacity, not FLOPs, set limits.
detail: Hence mixed precision, FlashAttention, quantization, paging.

q: Prefill vs decode?
short: Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel (compute-bound, determines TTFT) and fills the KV cache; decode generates one token at a time reading weights and cache (bandwidth-bound, determines TPOT).
detail: Chunked prefill interleaves them.

q: KV-cache size for 4096 tokens with 32 layers, width 4096, 16-bit?
short: 524,288 B/token × 4096 = 2 GiB per sequence.
detail: GQA-8 → 512 MiB.

q: When would you fine-tune rather than prompt?
short: When prompting can't reliably produce the needed behaviour, format or style, you have many good examples, latency or context cost matters, or you want a smaller model specialised; facts that change belong in retrieval.
detail: Try prompting first.

q: Which efficiency methods change outputs and which don't?
short: Output-preserving: FlashAttention, Ring Attention, KV caching, paged attention, continuous batching, speculative decoding. Can change outputs: quantization, pruning, sparse/linear attention, distillation, GQA/MQA (architecture change).
detail: Floating-point order can cause tiny differences.

q: Serve a 13B model with 32k context to 20 users on one 80 GB GPU.
short: Weights int4 ≈ 6.5 GB; KV per token with GQA-8 (40 layers, head 128, 16-bit) ≈ 160 KB → 32k ≈ 5 GB per user; 20 users ≈ 100 GB: too much, so quantize the KV cache to 8-bit (≈ 50 GB), use paged attention so actual lengths (not maximum) count, and continuous batching.
detail: Real lengths are usually much shorter.
follow: What if users max out context?

q: Why do we scale attention scores by √d?
short: Dot products of d-dimensional random vectors have variance ∝ d; without scaling, large scores saturate softmax into near one-hot weights with tiny gradients. Dividing by √d keeps variance ≈ 1.
detail: Original Transformer.

q: MoE vs dense at equal per-token compute?
short: MoE has more total parameters (more capacity, often better quality) at the same per-token FLOPs, but needs memory for all experts, load balancing and communication; dense is simpler to train and serve.
detail: Active vs total.
mistakes: Comparing active MoE size to dense total.

q: Estimate 3B full fine-tuning vs QLoRA memory (before activations).
short: Full: 3 × 16 = 48 GB. QLoRA: 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 GB base + small LoRA states (a few hundred MB) ≈ 2 GB.
detail: Activations extra.
mistakes: Forgetting optimizer states in full FT.

q: How do scaling laws influence architecture and data choices?
short: They predict loss from N, D and C, letting teams pick model size and token count before training (Chinchilla balance), justify data collection and deduplication, and decide when to over-train small models for cheaper inference.
detail: Fit on small runs, extrapolate.
mistakes: Assuming loss predicts every downstream skill.

q: Trace one token from prompt to output.
short: Tokenize (BPE) → embed → for each layer: RMSNorm → attention with RoPE on q/k (reading/writing the KV cache) → residual → RMSNorm → SwiGLU/MoE → residual → final norm → logits → temperature/top-p → sample → append and repeat.
detail: Prefill does this for all prompt tokens at once.

q: Speculative decoding: α = 0.9, k = 4. Tokens per pass?
detail: Speed-up also depends on draft cost.

q: Budget: 10²³ FLOPs. Plan model size and data.
short: Chinchilla-style: C = 6ND with D ≈ 20N → N ≈ √(C/120) ≈ 29B, D ≈ 0.58T tokens; for a heavily used product, choose a smaller N (e.g. 10B) with more tokens (1.7T). Ensure enough deduplicated data; plan memory (16 B/param sharded), mixed precision, FlashAttention.
detail: Fitted laws may shift the ratio.
example: M2's Hoffmann fit gave a higher ratio.

q: Where do the first-half methods conflict?
short: MoE raises memory while cutting compute; quantization saves memory but can hurt reasoning; larger batches cut cost but raise latency; long context increases KV and attention cost; fine-tuning specialises but can erode safety and general skills.
detail: Design = choosing trade-offs.

q: Why does long context stress both training and serving?
short: Training: attention n² compute and activation memory (FlashAttention, Ring Attention, RoPE scaling). Serving: KV cache linear in n per user and read every step (GQA/MLA, cache quantization, paging).
detail: Plus quality: models must learn to use far context.

q: A client wants a cheap domain assistant. Outline the stack.
short: Start from a strong open base; retrieval for documents; SFT via LoRA on curated domain dialogues; preference tuning (M9) if needed; quantize to int4/int8; serve with continuous batching and paged KV; evaluate quality, safety, latency and cost.
detail: Iterate with real usage.

q: What changes in the second half?
short: Focus moves from building and running models to shaping and using them: preference alignment, prompting and reasoning, retrieval, agents, evaluation, safety and multimodality; the first-half costs (context length, decoding, serving) constrain all of these.
detail: E.g. RAG increases prompt length and TTFT.
example: Agents call the model many times.
follow: How do agents change serving load?
